section_1a.directions: Section I, Part A — Multiple Choice: 55 questions, 55 minutes. Each question is followed by four answer choices. Select the choice that best answers the question or completes the statement. This part counts for 40 percent of the exam score. Work briskly; all questions count equally.

items.explanation: Murray wrote while talk of natural rights and equality filled the air. Her essay took those revolutionary principles and applied them to women, arguing that if liberty was a natural right, women deserved education and fairer treatment under the law. That borrowing of revolutionary ideas for women's claims is the development being illustrated. Option A is wrong because women's voting remained extremely rare after independence; New Jersey allowed some women to vote for a time, then revoked the right in 1807. Option C is wrong because coverture, the law that placed a wife's legal identity under her husband's, survived the Revolution intact. Option D is wrong because Congress created no general pension policy for women soldiers.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: only New Jersey briefly allowed women to vote, and it revoked the right in 1807; most states never did.
option_explanations.B: Correct: Murray applied the Revolution's natural-rights reasoning to argue for women's education and legal standing.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: coverture remained the law after the Revolution; the essay argued against such inequalities but did not end them.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: there was no general congressional pension program for women who served.

options: (A) Most states granted women full voting rights after independence, extending the Revolution's promise of equality to the ballot box.
(B) Some women used the Revolution's language of natural rights to press for women's education and fairer laws.
(C) The Revolution abolished the legal doctrine of coverture throughout the nation.
(D) Congress established military pensions for women who had served as soldiers.
items.stem: Murray's argument best illustrates which of the following developments in revolutionary-era America?
items.stimulus: In 1790 Judith Sargent Murray published the essay "On the Equality of the Sexes," arguing that women's minds were equal to men's and that girls deserved the same education as boys. Source: Judith Sargent Murray, "On the Equality of the Sexes," 1790 (public domain).

items.explanation: Republican motherhood gave women an indirect political role: because the republic needed virtuous citizens, mothers performed a civic service by raising sons who would value liberty and reject corruption. Women's influence ran through the family rather than through the ballot box or officeholding. Option A is wrong because women did not win legislative seats in this era. Option B is wrong because married women's property remained under their husbands' control under coverture. Option C is wrong because organized national woman suffrage campaigns did not appear until the mid-1800s, beginning with Seneca Falls in 1848.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: women held no legislative seats in the early republic.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: coverture kept a wife's property under her husband's legal control.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: national suffrage organizing came decades later, starting at Seneca Falls in 1848.
option_explanations.D: Correct: republican motherhood cast mothers as teachers of the civic virtue the republic required.

options: (A) Women won seats in state legislatures across the new nation.
(B) Married women gained full legal control over the property and wages they earned during marriage, ending the doctrine of coverture in the early republic.
(C) Women organized national campaigns demanding the vote.
(D) Women were expected to shape the republic by teaching civic virtue to their children, the republic's future citizens.
items.stem: Which of the following best describes the political role that the idea of republican motherhood assigned to women?
items.stimulus: After the Revolution, writers such as Judith Sargent Murray and Benjamin Rush argued that the new republic depended on virtuous citizens, and that mothers, as children's first teachers, had a civic duty to raise sons loyal to republican ideals. Historians call this idea "republican motherhood."

items.explanation: Adams deliberately used the vocabulary of the patriot cause, words like tyrants and rebellion, to make her point. By echoing the language men used against the king, she argued that husbands who held unchecked power over wives were no better than the tyrants the Revolution opposed, and she pressed John Adams to write fairer laws. Option B is wrong because the letter contains no warning about British agents. Option C is wrong because she urged her husband to act but drafted no legislation herself. Option D is wrong because the letter discusses lawmaking and women's rights, not battlefield reports.

option_explanations.A: Correct: she borrowed the patriots' anti-tyranny rhetoric to pressure her husband on women's rights.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: the letter warns about husbands' power, not British spies.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: she urged action but wrote no draft laws.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: the letter is about laws and women's standing, not military news.

options: (A) She was using the patriots' own arguments against tyranny to press her husband for women's rights.
(B) She was warning John Adams that British agents in Philadelphia were plotting to arrest patriot leaders.
(C) She was drafting specific laws for the new state government to pass.
(D) She was reporting military news from the siege of Boston.
items.stem: Adams's choice of words such as "tyrants" suggests which of the following about her purpose in the letter?
items.stimulus: "Remember the Ladies, and be more generous and favorable to them than your ancestors. Do not put such unlimited power into the hands of the Husbands. Remember all Men would be tyrants if they could." Source: Abigail Adams, letter to John Adams, March 1776 (public domain).

items.explanation: Jefferson believed in a federal government of strictly limited powers, yet the Louisiana treaty offered land the Constitution never mentioned. His private admission that the Constitution made no provision for acquiring foreign territory captures the collision: his principles said no, while the bargain, control of the Mississippi, removal of a French neighbor, was too valuable to refuse. He went ahead anyway and asked Congress to fund it. Option A is wrong because Jefferson pursued the purchase eagerly; his doubt was about constitutional authority, not the deal itself. Option B is wrong because New England Federalists opposed the purchase, fearing new western states would dilute their influence. Option D is wrong because the Supreme Court never ruled on the purchase's constitutionality.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: Jefferson wanted the territory; he questioned only whether the Constitution authorized the purchase.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: Federalists opposed the purchase as a threat to their region's power.
option_explanations.C: Correct: his limited-government principles conflicted with an opportunity he would not pass up.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: the Court never declared the purchase unconstitutional.

options: (A) Jefferson opposed buying Louisiana and tried to cancel the treaty.
(B) Federalists in New England celebrated the purchase as a great victory for their party's commercial and political interests.
(C) Jefferson's limited-government principles clashed with a territorial bargain he would not pass up.
(D) The Supreme Court declared the Louisiana Purchase unconstitutional.
items.stem: Jefferson's private doubt about the Louisiana Purchase best illustrates which of the following?
items.stimulus: "The Constitution has made no provision for our holding foreign territory, still less for incorporating foreign nations into our Union." Source: Thomas Jefferson, letter to John Breckinridge, August 1803 (public domain; via Founders Online).

items.explanation: The purchase promised a flood of new western states, and those states would be agrarian and likely Democratic-Republican. New England Federalists, already losing ground nationally, saw their region's share of House seats and electoral votes shrinking and their commercial, pro-British outlook swamped by an expanding agrarian republic. Opposition was about political survival, not the price. Option A is wrong because Southern planters welcomed new land for slavery's expansion. Option C is wrong because western farmers were the purchase's biggest winners, gaining the Mississippi and New Orleans. Option D is wrong because Democratic-Republican leaders backed Jefferson's treaty.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: Southern planters supported expansion that could extend plantation agriculture.
option_explanations.B: Correct: Federalists feared new western states would shrink New England's weight in Congress.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: western farmers gained the most, securing the Mississippi trade route.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: Democratic-Republicans backed the treaty.

options: (A) Southern planters, who feared that cheap new western lands would undercut the value of their own plantations.
(B) New England Federalists, who feared new western states would dilute their influence in Congress.
(C) Western farmers, who opposed American control of New Orleans.
(D) Democratic-Republican leaders, who considered the price too high.
items.stem: Which of the following groups was most likely to oppose the Louisiana Purchase, and why?
items.stimulus: The 1803 Louisiana Purchase doubled the size of the United States for $15 million, giving American farmers control of the Mississippi River and the port of New Orleans.

items.explanation: No candidate won a majority of electoral votes in 1824, so the Twelfth Amendment sent the choice to the House, which voted by state delegation among the top three finishers. Jackson had led in both the popular vote and the electoral college, but the House delegations chose Adams 13 to 7 to 4. Jackson's supporters called the result a corrupt bargain when Adams named Henry Clay, who had backed him in the House, as secretary of state. Option A is wrong because Jackson lost the House vote and did not become president until 1828. Option B is wrong because Adams trailed Jackson in the popular vote. Option C is wrong because Crawford, though ill, remained one of the three candidates the House considered.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: Jackson lost in 1824 and won the presidency in 1828.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: Adams trailed Jackson in the popular vote.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: Crawford was one of the three candidates the House considered.
option_explanations.D: Correct: the House chose Adams although Jackson had led in both popular and electoral votes.

options: (A) Andrew Jackson won the presidency in 1824.
(B) John Quincy Adams won a majority of the popular vote.
(C) William H. Crawford withdrew from the race before the House of Representatives cast its votes.
(D) The House chose Adams even though Jackson had led in popular and electoral votes.
items.stem: The table best supports which of the following conclusions about the election of 1824?
items.stimulus: Vote in the House of Representatives, February 1825 (each state delegation cast one vote): John Quincy Adams, 13 states; Andrew Jackson, 7 states; William H. Crawford, 4 states. (Jackson had led in both the popular vote and the electoral college.)

items.explanation: During the 1820s and 1830s, state after state dropped property qualifications for voting, opening the franchise to nearly all adult white men. New mass parties then competed fiercely for these new voters with rallies, parades, and partisan newspapers, driving turnout sharply upward through the Jacksonian era. Option B is wrong because women did not gain voting rights in this period. Option C is wrong because the Fifteenth Amendment came in 1870, decades later. Option D is wrong because direct election of senators arrived with the Seventeenth Amendment in 1913.

option_explanations.A: Correct: dropping property requirements enfranchised far more white men, and party competition mobilized them.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: women's suffrage did not arrive until 1920.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: the Fifteenth Amendment was ratified in 1870.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: senators were still chosen by state legislatures until 1913.

options: (A) States removed property requirements, allowing far more white men to vote.
(B) Women gained the right to vote nationwide.
(C) The Fifteenth Amendment, ratified after the Civil War, enfranchised Black men throughout the South.
(D) Senators began to be elected directly by the voters.
items.stem: Which of the following best explains the sharp rise in voter turnout between 1824 and 1840?
items.stimulus: In the presidential election of 1824, roughly one quarter of eligible voters cast ballots. By 1840, turnout had risen to about four-fifths of eligible voters.

items.explanation: Jackson's supporters believed the House had stolen the 1824 election through an elite deal. Martin Van Buren harnessed that anger by building the Democratic Party into a disciplined national organization with local committees, allied newspapers, and get-out-the-vote machinery aimed at ordinary voters. Politics became a mass-participation contest, the core of the Second Party System. Option A is wrong because the Whig Party formed in the mid-1830s to oppose Jackson, not immediately after 1824. Option B is wrong because turnout rose sharply, not fell. Option D is wrong because sectional disagreements over tariffs, banks, and slavery intensified in these years.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: the Whigs organized in the mid-1830s against Jackson, not right after 1824.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: voter participation climbed steeply in the Jacksonian era.
option_explanations.C: Correct: Jacksonian organizers built mass parties that mobilized ordinary voters.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: sectional conflict deepened rather than ending.

options: (A) The immediate creation of the Whig Party as the main opposition to Andrew Jackson's presidency.
(B) A long decline in voter participation.
(C) The rise of mass political parties that mobilized ordinary voters.
(D) An end to sectional disagreements.
items.stem: The anger of Jackson's supporters after 1824 most directly contributed to which of the following?
items.stimulus: Outraged by the "corrupt bargain," Jackson's supporters built statewide committees, allied newspapers, and voter-mobilization drives behind Martin Van Buren's organization, turning the Democratic Party into a disciplined national machine.

items.explanation: Jackson argued that the Bank's federal charter gave a small group of wealthy stockholders special privileges, letting the rich bend government to selfish ends. In his strict view, such an institution exceeded what the federal government should do and concentrated economic power dangerously. The veto became a defining statement of Jacksonian hostility to federally sponsored economic privilege. Option A is wrong because federally promoted banks and tariffs were Henry Clay's American System, which Jackson opposed. Option C is wrong because Jackson objected to the Bank's privilege and power, not its size; he favored state banks and hard money instead. Option D is wrong because the veto message addressed banking, not tariff rates.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: promoting banks and tariffs was Clay's American System, which Jackson rejected.
option_explanations.B: Correct: Jackson saw the Bank as concentrated privilege beyond proper federal power.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: he opposed the Bank's special privileges, not its size; he preferred state banks.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: the message concerned the Bank, not tariff policy.

options: (A) The federal government should actively promote American manufacturing through protective tariffs and a national bank.
(B) A national bank concentrated special privilege and exceeded the federal government's proper limits.
(C) The Bank was too small and needed a larger federal subsidy.
(D) High tariffs were necessary to protect American workers.
items.stem: Jackson's veto message reflects which of the following views of federal power?
items.stimulus: "It is to be regretted that the rich and powerful too often bend the acts of government to their selfish purposes." Source: Andrew Jackson, veto message on the recharter of the Bank of the United States, July 1832 (public domain).

items.explanation: The Erie Canal and the flood of migrants into western New York uprooted people from settled communities and their established churches. In that fluid, fast-changing setting, traveling evangelists like Charles Grandison Finney found eager audiences, and new movements, from Mormonism to Adventism to utopian communes, took hold. Social disruption, not stability, bred religious innovation. Option A is wrong because New York had disestablished its state church; no law required membership. Option B is wrong because the region's settlers were overwhelmingly native-born Protestants, not Catholics. Option C is wrong because the canal connected the region to national markets; that very connection drove the upheaval.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: New York had no established church requiring membership.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: the migrants were mainly native-born Protestants.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: the Erie Canal linked the region to markets; connection, not isolation, drove change.
option_explanations.D: Correct: rapid settlement and new transportation links broke up older community structures, opening space for new movements.

options: (A) State laws requiring church membership.
(B) The dominance of Catholic immigrants in the region.
(C) The region's isolation from national transportation and communication networks in the early 1800s.
(D) Rapid settlement and new transportation links that broke up older community structures.
items.stem: The Burned-Over District's burst of new religious movements was most directly facilitated by which of the following?
items.stimulus: In the 1820s and 1830s, western New York, crossed by the new Erie Canal and crowded with migrants, became known as the "Burned-Over District" because waves of religious revivals swept through it, producing new movements such as Mormonism and Seventh-day Adventism.

items.explanation: The Mormons did not move west for land or gold; they fled. Mob violence and the murder of Joseph Smith in Illinois convinced Brigham Young that the community could survive only by leaving the United States for an isolated valley where it could govern itself. The trek repeated a familiar American pattern: a persecuted religious group using western migration as an escape. Option B is wrong because the Homestead Act came in 1862, fifteen years later. Option C is wrong because the Mormons arrived in 1847 seeking refuge, not gold, which was discovered in California in 1848. Option D is wrong because no federal program relocated them; they organized and funded the migration themselves.

option_explanations.A: Correct: persecution pushed the Mormons to seek refuge through westward migration.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: the Homestead Act was passed in 1862, well after the 1847 trek.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: the Mormons sought isolation and safety, not California gold.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: the migration was organized by the Mormons themselves, not the government.

options: (A) Religious persecution driving a community to seek refuge through western migration.
(B) The Homestead Act drawing settlers west with offers of free federal land for family farms.
(C) The California gold rush pulling migrants westward.
(D) A federal program relocating religious minorities.
items.stem: The Mormon migration to the Great Salt Lake valley best illustrates which of the following patterns?
items.stimulus: After Joseph Smith was killed in Illinois in 1844, Brigham Young led thousands of Mormons westward; in 1847 they founded Salt Lake City in the Great Salt Lake valley, then part of Mexico.

items.explanation: The Mormon pioneers blazed and improved overland trails, established way stations, and proved that large groups could settle the arid Far West permanently. Their organized migration added a major stream to the westward movement of the 1840s and 1850s. Option A is wrong because Utah did not become a state until 1896, partly because of conflicts over polygamy. Option B is wrong because disputes with federal authority continued, flaring into the Utah War of 1857-1858. Option D is wrong because Mormons remained politically active, organizing the territory and later seeking statehood.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: Utah achieved statehood in 1896, not the 1840s.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: the Utah War of 1857-1858 showed conflict continued.
option_explanations.C: Correct: the Mormon trek strengthened overland routes and Far West settlement.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: Mormons stayed politically organized and pursued statehood.

options: (A) Utah's immediate admission as a state.
(B) An end to conflicts between Mormon settlers and the federal government over territorial control.
(C) The expansion of overland migration routes and settlement in the Far West.
(D) The Mormons' complete withdrawal from national politics and public affairs for the remainder of the century.
items.stem: The Mormon settlement of Utah in the late 1840s most directly contributed to which of the following?

items.explanation: The Free Soilers were not abolitionists seeking to end slavery where it existed; they were mostly Northerners who wanted the West kept open for small farmers working their own land. They argued that allowing slavery into the territories would let wealthy planters monopolize the best land and degrade the dignity of free labor. Keeping slavery out protected white workers' opportunity. Option A is wrong because the party deliberately avoided demanding abolition in the South. Option C is wrong because the platform opposed planter interests. Option D is wrong because deportation to Africa was the colonization movement's goal, not the Free Soilers'.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: Free Soilers did not demand immediate abolition in the Southern states.
option_explanations.B: Correct: they wanted western lands reserved for free white labor, not slave labor.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: the slogan opposed planter expansion, not protected it.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: African colonization was a separate movement's goal.

options: (A) Demanded the immediate abolition of slavery in the Southern states.
(B) Wanted western territories reserved for free white workers rather than slave labor.
(C) Sought to protect the profits of Southern plantations.
(D) Planned to deport enslaved people to Africa and resettle them in colonies established abroad.
items.stem: The Free Soil slogan indicates that the party opposed the expansion of slavery primarily because its supporters
items.stimulus: "Free Soil, Free Speech, Free Labor and Free Men." Source: Slogan of the Free Soil Party, 1848 (public domain).

items.explanation: By letting each territory's settlers vote on slavery, the act threw the question open in Kansas. Proslavery Missourians and antislavery New Englanders rushed in, each side determined to win the vote, and the territory descended into raids, sacked towns, and political violence known as Bleeding Kansas. Option A is wrong because Kansas remained a territory in 1854 and entered the Union as a free state in 1861. Option B is wrong because the Fugitive Slave Act stayed in force. Option C is wrong because the Democratic Party survived, though badly split by 1860.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: Kansas was organized as a territory in 1854 and became a state in 1861.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: the Fugitive Slave Act was not repealed.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: the Democratic Party endured, splitting only in 1860.
option_explanations.D: Correct: popular sovereignty triggered violent conflict between settler factions in Kansas.

options: (A) Kansas entered the Union as a free state in 1854 after antislavery settlers won the territorial vote.
(B) Congress repealed the Fugitive Slave Act.
(C) The Democratic Party dissolved.
(D) Armed clashes erupted between proslavery and antislavery settlers in Kansas.
items.stem: Which of the following was the most direct consequence of the Kansas-Nebraska Act?
items.stimulus: The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 let settlers in the Kansas and Nebraska territories vote on whether to allow slavery, repealing the Missouri Compromise's ban on slavery north of 36°30′.

items.explanation: Free Soilers accepted slavery where it already existed but drew a line at its spread, hoping that confining it would put it on the path to eventual extinction. The Republican platform of 1860 took exactly that position: no slavery in the territories, no interference with slavery in the Southern states. The strategy was containment, not immediate destruction. Option B is wrong because Garrison demanded immediate, uncompensated emancipation everywhere, a far more radical position. Option C is wrong because secession was the South's response to that containment strategy. Option D is wrong because popular sovereignty let settlers decide, while Free Soilers wanted Congress to ban slavery from the territories.

option_explanations.A: Correct: both sought to contain slavery's expansion without abolishing it where it existed.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: Garrison demanded immediate emancipation everywhere, not containment.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: secession defended slavery's expansion; Free Soilers opposed it.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: popular sovereignty let settlers vote, while Free Soilers wanted a congressional ban.

options: (A) The Republican platform of 1860, which opposed slavery's expansion while accepting it where it existed.
(B) William Lloyd Garrison's demand for the immediate, uncompensated emancipation of all enslaved people everywhere in the United States.
(C) The Southern states' decision to secede in 1860-1861.
(D) The doctrine of popular sovereignty.
items.stem: The Free Soil Party's strategy toward slavery was most similar to which of the following?

items.explanation: After the Civil War, Washington promoted western settlement through the Homestead Act of 1862, which offered 160 acres to settlers, and through enormous land grants to railroad companies building transcontinental lines. The army simultaneously waged campaigns that confined Native nations to reservations, clearing the way for those settlers. What the government did not do in this period was finance irrigation: large-scale federal water projects in the arid West began only with the Reclamation Act of 1902. Option A describes the real Homestead Act. Option B describes the real Pacific Railway land grants. Option C describes the real reservation policy enforced by the army.

option_explanations.A: True: the Homestead Act of 1862 granted 160 acres to settlers.
option_explanations.B: True: railroad companies received vast land grants for transcontinental lines.
option_explanations.C: True: the army confined Native nations to reservations.
option_explanations.D: Correct as the exception: federally funded irrigation projects began with the Reclamation Act of 1902, not in 1860-1890.

options: (A) Granting public land to settlers under the Homestead Act.
(B) Giving land grants to companies building transcontinental railroads.
(C) Using the army to confine Native nations to reservations.
(D) Paying for large-scale irrigation projects across the arid West.
items.stem: Between 1860 and 1890, the federal government encouraged western settlement in all of the following ways EXCEPT

items.explanation: The proviso never passed, but its proposal mattered enormously: for the first time, Congress seriously debated banning slavery from a vast new territory, and the debate revealed that every future land acquisition would reopen the slavery question. From 1846 on, expansion and slavery could not be discussed separately. Option A is wrong because the proviso failed repeatedly in the Senate. Option C is wrong because Southern congressmen fiercely opposed it as an attack on their rights. Option D is wrong because the debate it started intensified through the Compromise of 1850, Kansas-Nebraska, and secession.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: the proviso never passed Congress.
option_explanations.B: Correct: the Mexican Cession made slavery's expansion the central political question.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: Southerners opposed the proviso vehemently.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: the slavery debate grew more bitter after 1846, not settled.

options: (A) Congress successfully banned slavery in all western territories.
(B) Acquiring Mexican territory forced slavery's expansion to the center of national politics.
(C) Southern congressmen supported restricting slavery's spread.
(D) The slavery debate was permanently settled when Congress rejected the proviso before the Mexican War ended.
items.stem: The Wilmot Proviso is most significant as evidence that
items.stimulus: "Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude shall ever exist in any part of said territory." Source: The Wilmot Proviso, proposed in Congress, 1846 (public domain).

items.explanation: O'Sullivan wrote as a Democratic journalist, and his providential language became the slogan of Polk's expansionist program: the annexation of Texas, the settlement of Oregon, and the war that took California and the Southwest. Democrats embraced expansion as the party's mission; their opponents did not. Option A is wrong because many Whigs, including Abraham Lincoln, condemned the Mexican War as an unjust land grab. Option B is wrong because abolitionists feared expansion would spread slavery, not fulfill a mission. Option D is wrong because the Federalist Party had collapsed by the 1820s.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: Whigs generally opposed the Mexican War and Polk's expansionism.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: abolitionists worried expansion would extend slavery.
option_explanations.C: Correct: Democrats adopted manifest destiny as the justification for Polk's territorial program.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: the Federalist Party no longer existed in 1845.

options: (A) Whigs who opposed the Mexican War as an aggressive land grab.
(B) Abolitionists who focused on ending slavery rather than on expanding the nation's territory.
(C) Democrats who backed James K. Polk's program of territorial expansion.
(D) Federalists who favored a strong central government.
items.stem: O'Sullivan's "manifest destiny" argument was most enthusiastically embraced by which of the following?
items.stimulus: "It is our manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence for the free development of our yearly multiplying millions." Source: John L. O'Sullivan, 1845 (public domain).

items.explanation: The carpetbag throne is a mocking symbol: it presents Grant as propped up by Northern opportunists rather than by legitimate Southern support. The cartoon speaks for Southern whites who saw Reconstruction governments as corrupt impositions run by outsiders, backed by federal bayonets, and resented both the newcomers and the policies that empowered them. Option B is wrong because the image is satirical and hostile, not admiring. Option C is wrong because the cartoonist opposed the federal presence; he did not ask for more of it. Option D is wrong because the cartoon treats the Northerners as profiteers, not heroes.

option_explanations.A: Correct: the cartoon voices Southern resentment of Reconstruction as outsider rule.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: the image mocks Grant rather than praising him.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: the cartoonist opposed federal intervention, not demanded more.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: the Northerners are shown as profiteers, not heroes.

options: (A) Reconstruction imposed an outsider-dominated government on the South that Southerners resented.
(B) Grant's administration was free of corruption and deserved praise.
(C) The South needed a larger occupying army.
(D) Northern migrants in the South were heroic defenders of freedpeople who bravely faced Southern hostility.
items.stem: The cartoonist's depiction of Grant most clearly expresses which of the following viewpoints?
items.stimulus: An 1872 cartoon in Puck magazine shows President Ulysses S. Grant seated on a throne shaped like a carpetbag, surrounded by Northern newcomers profiting in the Reconstruction South.

items.explanation: The war had wrecked the Southern economy, but Reconstruction created openings: federal offices, military contracts, teaching posts in new freedpeople's schools, and cheap land and business opportunities. Ambitious Northerners moved south to fill them, which is why Southern whites scorned them as carpetbaggers. Option A is wrong because the Homestead Act offered western, not Southern, land. Option B is wrong because no draft ordered civilians to relocate. Option C is wrong because Southern white governments resisted Northern involvement rather than inviting it.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: the Homestead Act applied to western public lands.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: there was no draft requiring relocation.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: Southern white leaders opposed Northern involvement.
option_explanations.D: Correct: economic openings and federal jobs drew Northerners south.

options: (A) Free farmland offered under the Homestead Act.
(B) Military draft orders requiring relocation.
(C) Invitations from Southern state governments asking Northerners to come register Black voters.
(D) Economic opportunities and federal jobs in the war-damaged South.
items.stem: During Reconstruction, Northerners who moved South ("carpetbaggers") were drawn primarily by which of the following?

items.explanation: Grant's defenders, facing Liberal Republican charges of corruption and bayonet rule, argued that the job was unfinished: white Southern terror groups like the Ku Klux Klan were murdering and intimidating Black voters, and only federal power, troops, marshals, and the Enforcement Acts, could protect the rights the amendments promised. The defense rested on the freedpeople's need for protection. Option A is wrong because even Republicans admitted Reconstruction faced violent resistance and incomplete results. Option C is wrong because Grant's supporters defended federal intervention; leaving the South alone was the Liberal Republicans' position. Option D is wrong because Republicans championed the Fifteenth Amendment, not its repeal.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: Republicans acknowledged violent resistance showed the work was incomplete.
option_explanations.B: Correct: they argued federal protection remained necessary for freedpeople's rights.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: that was the Liberal Republican position, not Grant's defense.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: Republicans supported the Fifteenth Amendment.

options: (A) Reconstruction had fully achieved all its goals.
(B) Federal protection was still necessary to secure the rights of freedpeople.
(C) Southern states should rebuild entirely on their own, without any federal help or interference.
(D) The Fifteenth Amendment should be repealed.
items.stem: Supporters of President Grant would most likely have defended his Southern policy by arguing that
items.stimulus: In 1872 a faction calling itself the Liberal Republicans broke with President Grant, nominating Horace Greeley and denouncing corruption and continued federal intervention in the South.

items.explanation: The platform's planks, public ownership of railroads, silver coinage to expand the money supply, and a graduated income tax, all required Washington to act against private concentrations of wealth. Populists concluded that farmers, squeezed by railroad rates and falling prices, could not bargain with giant corporations on their own; only federal power matched corporate power. Option A is wrong because the platform demanded intervention, the opposite of laissez-faire. Option B is wrong because Populists wanted to save farming, not abandon it. Option D is wrong because the Supreme Court had already limited state regulation of interstate railroads in Wabash v. Illinois (1886).

option_explanations.A: Wrong: the platform demanded government action, not unregulated markets.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: Populists sought to rescue farmers, not move them to factories.
option_explanations.C: Correct: Populists believed only federal power could check corporate power.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: states could not effectively regulate interstate railroads after Wabash (1886).

options: (A) Unregulated markets would solve farmers' problems on their own.
(B) Farmers should abandon agriculture for factory work.
(C) Only the federal government was strong enough to check concentrated corporate power.
(D) Individual states could effectively regulate interstate railroads, making federal intervention unnecessary for farmers' grievances.
items.stem: The Omaha Platform's demands show that Populists believed which of the following?
items.stimulus: The People's Party's 1892 Omaha Platform demanded government ownership of the railroads and telegraphs, the free coinage of silver, and a graduated income tax.

items.explanation: The Populists demanded a graduated federal income tax in 1892; the Sixteenth Amendment, ratified in 1913, finally authorized one. Other Populist planks also became law later, including the direct election of senators. The platform's ideas outlived the party. Option B is wrong because railroad regulation increased, not ended, in the twentieth century. Option C is wrong because Populists wanted silver coinage, the opposite of a permanent gold standard. Option D is wrong because direct election of senators was adopted, not repealed, in the Seventeenth Amendment.

option_explanations.A: Correct: the Sixteenth Amendment (1913) realized the Populist income-tax plank.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: federal railroad regulation grew stronger, not weaker.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: Populists wanted free silver, the opposite of the gold standard.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: direct election of senators was adopted in the Seventeenth Amendment.

options: (A) The Sixteenth Amendment, which authorized a federal income tax.
(B) The end of all federal railroad regulation.
(C) The permanent adoption of the gold standard.
(D) The repeal of direct election of senators and a return to selection by state legislatures.
items.stem: Which of the following twentieth-century reforms fulfilled a demand first made in the Populists' Omaha Platform?

items.explanation: Donnelly charged that farmers' labor was being stolen to build colossal fortunes. The strongest support would pair the two halves of that charge: evidence that farmers received less and less for their crops while the railroads and creditors they depended on kept charging high rates. Falling prices plus rigid costs equals the squeeze Donnelly described. Option A is wrong because rising city wages say nothing about farmers' condition. Option C is wrong because Carnegie's libraries, however generous, do not address whether farmers were being crushed. Option D is wrong because rising total output alongside falling prices actually deepened farmers' troubles; it does not show who benefited.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: urban wage trends do not measure farmers' distress.
option_explanations.B: Correct: collapsing crop prices with steep freight rates documents the squeeze Donnelly described.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: Carnegie's philanthropy does not address farmers' economic condition.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: higher output with lower prices worsened, not eased, farmers' plight.

options: (A) Records showing that factory wages in Eastern cities rose steadily while farm income collapsed.
(B) Data showing crop prices collapsing while freight charges remained steep.
(C) Andrew Carnegie's donations to build public libraries.
(D) Statistics showing total American farm output increasing.
items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would best support Donnelly's claim that ordinary farmers were being crushed by powerful economic interests?
items.stimulus: Ignatius Donnelly wrote the People's Party 1892 Omaha Platform preamble, charging that "the fruits of the toil of millions are boldly stolen to build up colossal fortunes for a few." Between 1870 and the mid-1890s, the prices farmers received for staple crops fell by roughly half, while railroad freight rates and interest on farm mortgages stayed high.

items.explanation: Southern mills paid low wages and drew whole families into the mill villages, where children became an extra source of cheap labor. Because Southern states set high age thresholds weakly or enforced them poorly, owners could work children long hours at a fraction of adult pay. The system ran on the availability of vulnerable, inexpensive workers. Option A is wrong because no federal law required child hiring; the laws that existed tried to limit it. Option B is wrong because unions opposed child labor, seeing it as undercutting adult wages. Option C is wrong because adults were plentiful; children were hired because they were cheaper, not because adults were scarce.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: no law required hiring children; laws aimed to restrict it.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: unions fought child labor as a threat to adult wages.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: adults were available; children were hired because they cost less.
option_explanations.D: Correct: cheap child labor plus weak state limits drove the practice.

options: (A) Federal laws requiring mills to hire children.
(B) Labor unions demanding jobs for young workers.
(C) A severe shortage of adult workers willing to accept low-paying jobs in Southern cotton mills.
(D) Mill owners' demand for cheap labor combined with weak state limits on child work.
items.stem: The widespread employment of children in Southern cotton mills was primarily driven by which of the following?
items.stimulus: In Southern cotton-mill towns around 1900, whole families were hired as a unit: parents and children as young as seven or eight worked twelve-hour shifts tending spinning machines.

items.explanation: The National Child Labor Committee sent investigators into mills precisely to gather firsthand evidence, photographs, interviews, and sworn statements, that reformers could carry to legislatures and the public. The report is a window into that method: document the abuse, publicize it, and demand laws. Option A is wrong because the report exposed dangerous conditions, the opposite of safety. Option C is wrong because the investigation focused on children's work, not adult pay scales. Option D is wrong because the report describes investigators' work, not a strike.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: the report documented dangerous conditions, not safety.
option_explanations.B: Correct: the report shows reformers investigating abuses to push for legislation.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: adult wages were not the investigation's subject.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: the report covers an investigation, not a union strike.

options: (A) Proof that Southern mills were safe workplaces.
(B) Reformers' use of on-the-ground investigation to pressure lawmakers.
(C) A measurement of adult workers' wages.
(D) An account of successful union strikes that organized Southern cotton-mill workers in the Progressive Era.
items.stem: A historian studying how Progressive Era reformers pursued change would find this report most useful as evidence of which of the following?
items.stimulus: In 1909 investigators for the National Child Labor Committee toured cotton mills in the Carolinas, interviewed overseers, and published reports describing how mills evaded age limits.

items.explanation: Child-labor reformers spoke the language of moral uplift: children belonged in schools and homes, not factories, and society had a duty to protect the vulnerable. That evangelical sense of moral responsibility descended directly from the antebellum reformers, abolitionists, temperance crusaders, and others, who had been inspired by the Second Great Awakening to perfect society. Option A is wrong because Social Darwinists defended ruthless competition, the opposite of protective reform. Option B is wrong because 1920s business boosters celebrated the industrial order reformers attacked. Option D is wrong because the tax revolt opposed government action rather than demanding it.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: Social Darwinists defended competition; reformers sought to restrain it.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: 1920s boosters celebrated the industrial system reformers criticized.
option_explanations.C: Correct: both generations drew on evangelical moral-reform ideals.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: the tax revolt opposed government intervention.

options: (A) Gilded Age defenders of unregulated competition.
(B) 1920s business leaders who celebrated industrial prosperity and denounced government regulation.
(C) Antebellum abolitionists and temperance crusaders driven by evangelical reform ideals.
(D) 1970s activists who campaigned to cut property taxes.

items.explanation: Congress did try: it passed the Keating-Owen Act in 1916 banning interstate shipment of goods made by child labor, and a second tax-based law in 1919. The Supreme Court struck both down, ruling in Hammer v. Dagenhart (1918) and Bailey v. Drexel Furniture (1922) that regulating child labor exceeded Congress's commerce and taxing powers. Only after the Court's stance shifted in the late 1930s could the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 succeed. Option B is wrong because many states had passed child-labor laws; the problem was the lack of a national standard. Option C is wrong because reformers enjoyed broad public sympathy. Option D is wrong because Congress acted twice before the 1930s and was blocked by the courts.

option_explanations.A: Correct: the Court voided the 1916 and 1919 federal laws, delaying a national ban until 1938.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: many states had child-labor laws; no uniform national rule existed.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: the public broadly supported protecting children.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: Congress passed child-labor laws in 1916 and 1919.

options: (A) The Supreme Court had struck down earlier federal child-labor laws.
(B) No state had ever passed a child-labor law before 1938.
(C) The public broadly opposed any regulation of child work.
(D) Congress never attempted a federal child-labor law before the 1930s, leaving the issue entirely to states.

items.explanation: Beveridge wrapped expansion in providence: God had unfurled the American banner over new lands, so retreat would be a betrayal of a divine mission to carry liberty and civilization outward. The argument was moral and religious, not legal or economic. Option A is wrong because Beveridge never cited constitutional barriers; he brushed them aside. Option B is wrong because he demanded engagement abroad, the opposite of isolationism. Option C is wrong because his rhetoric assumed nonwhite peoples needed American uplift, not that they were already equal.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: Beveridge ignored constitutional objections to empire.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: he urged expansion abroad, not isolation.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: his language assumed other peoples needed American civilization.
option_explanations.D: Correct: he claimed Providence assigned Americans a civilizing mission.

options: (A) The Constitution forbade governing overseas territories.
(B) The United States should avoid all foreign entanglements and focus entirely on domestic concerns.
(C) All peoples were already equal and self-governing.
(D) Providence had assigned Americans a duty to spread their civilization.
items.stem: Beveridge's argument for American expansion rested primarily on which of the following beliefs?
items.stimulus: "We can not retreat from any soil where Providence has unfurled our banner; it is ours to save that soil for liberty and civilization." Source: Senator Albert Beveridge, "The March of the Flag," 1898 (public domain).

items.explanation: The League turned the Declaration of Independence against the imperialists: if governments derive just powers from the consent of the governed, then ruling Filipinos who had never consented was criminal aggression and a betrayal of the principles of Washington and Lincoln. Their case was about American identity, not ledgers. Option A is wrong because cost arguments were secondary to their principled claim. Option C is wrong because they argued the opposite, that the Constitution's principles forbade empire. Option D is wrong because they condemned European-style colonialism rather than copying it.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: their core argument was principle, not military expense.
option_explanations.B: Correct: they charged that ruling without consent betrayed America's founding ideals.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: they argued constitutional principles opposed colonial rule.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: they condemned European colonial methods.

options: (A) Would cost more in military spending than the colonies were worth.
(B) Betrayed America's founding principles by ruling Filipinos without their consent.
(C) Was required by the Constitution's grant of war powers.
(D) Should copy the colonial methods that European empires used to govern their possessions in Asia.

items.stimulus: "We hold that the policy known as imperialism is hostile to liberty and tends toward militarism... governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed." Source: American Anti-Imperialist League platform, 1899 (public domain).

items.explanation: The League organized specifically to fight the annexation of the Philippines after the Spanish-American War. Its members, including Mark Twain and William Jennings Bryan, argued that purchasing a colony of millions of Filipinos violated consent of the governed, and they lobbied the Senate to reject the Treaty of Paris. The treaty passed by one vote. Option A is wrong because anti-imperialists supported Cuban independence; they opposed keeping Cuba as a colony. Option B is wrong because the Open Door notes concerned trade access, not colonial rule. Option D is wrong because Hawaiian statehood came in 1959, long after the League's era.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: anti-imperialists favored Cuban independence.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: the Open Door notes addressed trade, not colonial annexation.
option_explanations.C: Correct: the League campaigned against Senate ratification of Philippine annexation.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: Hawaiian statehood came in 1959, decades later.

(B) The Open Door notes promising equal trading rights for all nations in China.
(C) The Senate's approval of the treaty annexing the Philippines.
(D) Hawaii's admission as a state.
items.stem: A member of the Anti-Imperialist League would most strongly have opposed which of the following?

items.explanation: Beveridge's claim that Providence assigned America a civilizing mission restated, for an overseas empire, what manifest destiny had claimed for the continent: that Americans were destined by God to spread their institutions across new lands. The geography changed from continent to globe; the providential logic did not. Option B is wrong because the Monroe Doctrine warned Europe against new colonization rather than blessing American empire. Option C is wrong because Washington warned against entangling alliances, a caution Beveridge ignored. Option D is wrong because Beveridge demanded expansion, the opposite of isolationism.

option_explanations.A: Correct: both claimed a God-given American mission to spread across new lands.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: the Monroe Doctrine warned Europe off, not authorized American empire.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: Washington warned against permanent alliances.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: Beveridge urged expansion, the opposite of isolationism.

options: (A) Manifest Destiny, the claim that Americans were destined to spread across the continent.
(B) The Monroe Doctrine's warning against new European colonization.
(C) Washington's Farewell Address and its warning against permanent alliances with foreign nations.
(D) Postwar isolationism.
items.stem: Beveridge's language of providence and national mission most directly continued which earlier American idea?

items.explanation: Long argued that the Depression persisted because wealth was hoarded by a few while millions lacked buying power. Share Our Wealth would cap fortunes at a few million dollars, tax inheritances steeply, and use the revenue to guarantee every family a home, a car, and a minimum income. The diagnosis pointed to redistribution as the cure. Option A is wrong because Long wanted massive new spending, not a balanced budget first. Option C is wrong because his plan expanded federal aid rather than ending it. Option D is wrong because the gold standard concerned money, not the distribution of wealth.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: Long proposed huge new spending, not budget balancing.
option_explanations.B: Correct: his plan taxed large fortunes to fund guaranteed incomes and homes.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: he wanted more federal relief, not less.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: the gold standard was unrelated to his redistribution plan.

options: (A) Balancing the federal budget before any new spending, since deficits threatened the nation's credit and economic recovery.
(B) Breaking up concentrated fortunes through federal redistribution.
(C) Ending all federal relief programs.
(D) A return to the gold standard.
items.stem: Long's Share Our Wealth program showed that he believed the Great Depression required which of the following?
items.stimulus: In 1934 Senator Huey Long launched the Share Our Wealth movement, proposing to cap personal fortunes, guarantee every family a home and an income, and fund it all with steep taxes on the rich.

items.explanation: Long attacked Roosevelt from the left, charging that the New Deal preserved the wealthy while ordinary people suffered. Other Depression-era critics made the same complaint from different directions, arguing that relief was too small and reform too timid. That put Long in the camp that wanted more government action, not less. Option A is wrong because Hoover's defenders said Roosevelt was doing too much. Option B is wrong because Prohibition's repeal was a separate issue already resolved in 1933. Option C is wrong because the Liberty League attacked the New Deal as dangerously radical, the opposite of Long's charge.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: Hoover's defenders thought Roosevelt went too far, not too little.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: Prohibition ended in 1933 and was unrelated to Long's critique.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: the Liberty League said the New Deal was too radical, the reverse of Long's charge.
option_explanations.D: Correct: like Long, they argued Roosevelt's programs did not go far enough.

options: (A) Defenders of Herbert Hoover's policies who insisted the Depression would cure itself without action.
(B) Advocates of Prohibition's repeal.
(C) Supporters of the Liberty League.
(D) Other Depression-era critics who argued the New Deal did not go far enough.
items.stem: Long's charge that Roosevelt was doing too little for ordinary Americans most resembled the criticism made by which of the following?

items.explanation: Four decades before Long, the Populists made the same case: railroads, banks, and trusts concentrated wealth while farmers and workers struggled, and only federal action could break that grip. Long's rhetoric of taking from the rich to aid the poor echoed the Omaha Platform's war on concentrated corporate power. Option B is wrong because Federalists favored elite-led order, not redistribution. Option C is wrong because the Know-Nothings organized around nativism, not wealth. Option D is wrong because Whigs promoted banks and economic development, the institutions Long attacked.

option_explanations.A: Correct: Long's attack on concentrated wealth echoed the Populist tradition.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: Federalists favored elite leadership, not redistribution.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: the Know-Nothings organized around nativism.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: Whigs promoted the banks and corporations Long attacked.

options: (A) The Populists of the 1890s.
(B) The Federalists of the 1790s.
(C) The Know-Nothings of the 1850s.
(D) The Whigs of the 1840s.

items.explanation: Truman spoke with Greece and Turkey in mind: both faced Soviet-backed pressure, Greece from a communist insurgency and Turkey from Soviet demands on the straits. His pledge turned the wartime analysis of Soviet expansionism into a standing American commitment to resist it. Option A is wrong because the doctrine committed the United States to action abroad, the opposite of avoidance. Option B is wrong because Truman pledged direct American support rather than leaving the task to the United Nations. Option D is wrong because the doctrine assumed communism was a grave threat.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: the doctrine committed the U.S. to overseas action.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: Truman pledged direct American aid, not UN action alone.
option_explanations.C: Correct: Soviet pressure on Greece and Turkey prompted the pledge.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: the doctrine treated communism as a serious threat.

options: (A) The United States should avoid all overseas commitments and return to a policy of strict neutrality.
(B) Only the United Nations should resist aggression.
(C) Soviet-backed pressure on countries like Greece and Turkey required a firm American answer.
(D) Communism posed no serious threat to American interests.

items.stimulus: "I believe that it must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures." Source: President Harry Truman, address to Congress, March 1947 (public domain).

items.explanation: Containment meant stopping communism's spread, and American planners believed poverty and chaos made Europeans vulnerable to communist appeals. The Marshall Plan poured aid into Western Europe's recovery so that stable, prosperous democracies would resist Soviet influence on their own. Option B is wrong because the Marshall Plan was economic aid to Europe, not a troop deployment to Asia. Option C is wrong because the United States did not cut off all trade with the Soviet bloc. Option D is wrong because the plan deepened American involvement in Europe, leading to NATO in 1949.

option_explanations.A: Correct: economic recovery was meant to make Western Europe resistant to communism.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: the plan was economic aid to Europe, not troops in Asia.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: the U.S. did not end all trade with the Soviet bloc.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: the plan deepened U.S. commitment to Europe.

options: (A) Rebuilt Western Europe's economies so communism would find fewer desperate recruits.
(B) Stationed American combat troops across Asia.
(C) Ended all American trade with the Soviet bloc.

items.explanation: Kennan argued that Soviet expansionism could be checked by steady, long-term pressure at every point where it pushed outward. Containment drew a line around existing communist power; it did not propose invading the Soviet Union or liberating Eastern Europe by force. Rollback, by contrast, meant pushing communism back where it already ruled. Option A is wrong because an immediate attack would be war, not containment. Option B is wrong because containment required constant vigilance and pressure. Option C is wrong because Kennan aimed to check Soviet power, not American power.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: a direct attack would mean war, the opposite of patient containment.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: containment demanded steady pressure, not indifference.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: Kennan sought to check Soviet expansion, not American power.
option_explanations.D: Correct: containment blocked further expansion without attempting to overthrow existing regimes.

options: (A) An immediate American military attack on the Soviet Union to destroy its regime before it could expand further into Europe.
(B) Ignoring Soviet actions entirely.
(C) Containing American power rather than Soviet power.
(D) Blocking further Soviet expansion without trying to overthrow communist regimes already in place.

items.stimulus: "It is a long-term, patient but firm and vigilant containment of Russian expansive tendencies." Source: George Kennan, "Long Telegram," 1946 (public domain; U.S. government document).

items.explanation: From 1949 on, the United States refused to recognize the People's Republic of China and blocked its admission to the United Nations, treating Beijing as an enemy to be isolated. Nixon's 1972 visit reversed that course: by opening relations with Mao's China, Washington split the communist world and moved from isolation to engagement. Option A is wrong because Korea applied containment to Asia rather than changing the China policy. Option C is wrong because the missile crisis concerned Cuba and the Soviet Union. Option D is wrong because the 1980 boycott was a late Cold War protest over Afghanistan, not a shift on China.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: Korea applied containment; it did not change China policy.
option_explanations.B: Correct: the 1972 visit ended isolation and opened engagement with Beijing.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: the missile crisis involved Cuba and the USSR, not China.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: the 1980 boycott protested the invasion of Afghanistan.

options: (A) American intervention in the Korean War.
(B) Nixon's 1972 visit to Beijing, which opened relations with the People's Republic of China.
(C) The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962.
(D) The American boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics in protest of the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan.

items.explanation: American leaders claimed to lead the free world against Soviet tyranny, yet Black Americans lived under segregation enforced by law and violence. Civil rights leaders seized on that contradiction: if America truly stood for liberty, it could not defend white supremacy at home. The argument embarrassed Washington and gave the movement moral leverage. Option A is wrong because King and others criticized American racism, not praised Soviet rights. Option B is wrong because the movement actively sought federal action, from court orders to legislation. Option D is wrong because the boycott challenged the whole system of segregation, not just fares.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: leaders highlighted American racism; they did not praise the USSR.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: the movement sought federal intervention, not its absence.
option_explanations.C: Correct: the Cold War made segregation a glaring contradiction of American ideals.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: the boycott targeted segregation itself, not bus fares.

options: (A) Praised the Soviet Union's record on civil rights as morally superior to the American record.
(B) Rejected any role for the federal government.
(C) Exposed the gap between America's promises of liberty and the reality of segregation.
(D) Focused only on lowering bus fares.

items.stimulus: In December 1955 Rosa Parks's arrest for refusing to give up her bus seat sparked a year-long Black boycott of Montgomery, Alabama's segregated buses, led by a young minister, Martin Luther King Jr.

items.explanation: Montgomery showed that disciplined nonviolence could fill jails, boycott businesses, and win in court without firing a shot. College students in Greensboro, Nashville, and Atlanta copied the model in 1960, sitting politely at whites-only lunch counters, accepting arrest, and training in nonviolent resistance. The sit-in movement was Montgomery's tactical heir. Option B is wrong because the late-1960s uprisings abandoned nonviolence. Option C is wrong because Black Power emphasized self-determination and often rejected integrationist nonviolence. Option D is wrong because filibusters were a Southern segregationist weapon in Congress, not a protest tactic.

option_explanations.A: Correct: the 1960 sit-ins copied Montgomery's disciplined nonviolent mass action.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: the urban uprisings rejected nonviolence.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: Black Power diverged from integrationist nonviolence.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: filibusters were used by segregationists in Congress.

options: (A) The 1960 student sit-ins at segregated Southern lunch counters.
(B) The urban uprisings of the late 1960s.
(C) The Black Power movement's separatism.
(D) Southern filibusters against civil rights bills conducted on the floor of the United States Senate.

items.explanation: Long before Montgomery, the NAACP had pursued equality through the courts, chipping at segregation case by case until Brown v. Board of Education (1954) declared school segregation unconstitutional. Browder v. Gayle, which ended bus segregation in Montgomery, extended that same legal strategy to public transportation. Option A is wrong because the Klan used terror against the movement. Option B is wrong because colonization sought to send Black Americans to Africa, a nineteenth-century idea. Option C is wrong because loyalty investigations targeted suspected communists, not segregation.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: the Klan terrorized civil rights supporters.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: colonization proposed removing Black Americans from the country.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: loyalty programs targeted suspected communists.
option_explanations.D: Correct: the court victory continued the NAACP's legal campaign.

options: (A) The Ku Klux Klan's campaign of intimidation.
(B) The nineteenth-century colonization movement.
(C) The federal loyalty investigations of suspected communists.
(D) The NAACP's decades-long legal challenge to segregation.

items.explanation: Friedan interviewed suburban housewives who had educations, comfortable homes, and healthy children yet felt restless and empty. She named that restlessness the feminine mystique: a culture that told women fulfillment came only through husband, children, and home, while closing off careers and public life. Option A is wrong because Friedan argued domesticity denied women professional fulfillment. Option C is wrong because she described political marginalization, not dominance. Option D is wrong because she criticized the narrowness of domestic life, not family itself.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: Friedan argued domesticity blocked professional fulfillment.
option_explanations.B: Correct: she described educated women feeling empty and cut off from wider purpose.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: she portrayed women as politically sidelined, not dominant.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: she criticized the narrowness of the homemaker role, not family life itself.

options: (A) Economically independent and professionally fulfilled.
(B) Unfulfilled, cut off from purposes beyond housework.
(C) Politically dominant in national elections.
(D) Determined to abandon their families entirely.

items.explanation: Friedan's book helped launch the modern women's movement: she co-founded the National Organization for Women in 1966, and activists pressed the government to enforce the new ban on sex discrimination in employment found in Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Equal employment opportunity became the movement's first great legal battleground. Option A is wrong because the Equal Rights Amendment passed Congress but was never ratified. Option B is wrong because women's suffrage had been won in 1920, decades earlier. Option D is wrong because no 1965 decision struck down all abortion restrictions; Griswold (1965) concerned contraception, and Roe v. Wade came in 1973.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: the ERA was never ratified.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: women won the vote in 1920.
option_explanations.C: Correct: Title VII (1964) banned sex discrimination in employment.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: the 1965 Griswold decision concerned contraception, not abortion.

options: (A) Ratification of the Equal Rights Amendment.
(B) Women's suffrage in federal elections.
(C) Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, banning sex discrimination in employment.

Each of the other developments pushed against that ideal. Option B is wrong as an answer because wartime factory work proved women could do industrial jobs. Option C is wrong as an answer because the New Woman pursued college, careers, and public life. Option D is wrong as an answer because the suffrage victory brought women into electoral politics.

option_explanations.A: Correct as the exception: the cult of domesticity reinforced traditional roles.
option_explanations.B: Not the exception: wartime factory work challenged domestic expectations.
option_explanations.C: Not the exception: the New Woman pursued education and public life.
option_explanations.D: Not the exception: suffrage brought women into politics.

questions.stimulus_text: World War I transformed the relationship between Americans and their government. The war gave Washington sweeping new powers to manage the economy, shape public opinion, and punish dissent. The Espionage Act of 1917 and the Sedition Act of 1918 made it a crime to criticize the war effort; Socialist leader Eugene Debs was sentenced to ten years in prison for a speech opposing the war. After the armistice, fear of radicals did not fade: Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer ordered raids that rounded up thousands of suspected communists and anarchists for deportation. Adapted from a secondary account of the World War I home front.
parts: A. Briefly explain ONE way in which World War I expanded the power of the federal government.
B. Briefly explain ONE way in which World War I led to the suppression of dissent in the United States.
C. Briefly explain ONE similarity between the federal government's treatment of dissent during World War I and its treatment of dissent in another period of American history.

exemplar.A: The war led Congress and President Wilson to create agencies that managed the wartime economy on an unprecedented scale, such as the War Industries Board directing factory production and the Food Administration urging conservation, which put the federal government in direct control of economic life.
exemplar.B: The Espionage and Sedition Acts criminalized criticism of the war, and the Supreme Court upheld convictions under them in Schenck v. United States (1919), so opponents of the war such as Eugene Debs were imprisoned for their speeches.
exemplar.C: During the Second Red Scare of the early Cold War, the federal government again traded liberty for security: loyalty programs, HUAC hearings, and Senator Joseph McCarthy's accusations punished suspected communists much as the Palmer Raids had punished suspected radicals after World War I.

questions.stimulus_text: "We meet in the midst of a nation brought to the verge of moral, political, and material ruin. Corruption dominates the ballot-box, the Legislatures, the Congress.... The fruits of the toil of millions are badly stolen to build up colossal fortunes for a few, unprecedented in the history of mankind; and the possessors of these, in turn, despise the Republic and endanger liberty. From the same prolific womb of governmental injustice we breed the two great classes, tramps and millionaires." Source: Ignatius Donnelly, preamble to the People's (Populist) Party platform, Omaha, 1892 (public domain).
parts: A. Briefly explain ONE reason farmers organized into the Populist movement in the late 1800s.
B. Briefly explain how ONE specific demand of the Populists reflected the grievances expressed in the passage.
C. Briefly explain ONE way in which Populist ideas influenced the United States in the years after the movement's decline.

exemplar.A: Farmers were squeezed between falling crop prices and high railroad freight rates and mortgage interest they could not control, so they organized through the Farmers' Alliances and then the People's Party to demand government action.
exemplar.B: The platform's demand for government ownership of the railroads directly answered Donnelly's charge that corrupt alliances between business and government produced 'tramps and millionaires,' by putting the railroads under public control.
exemplar.C: The Sixteenth Amendment (1913), authorizing a federal income tax, enacted the Omaha Platform's graduated income-tax plank, showing Populist ideas living on in Progressive Era reform.

exemplar.C: The early-1900s Texas oil boom transformed the Gulf Southwest: gushers at Spindletop (1901) drew workers and investment, built Houston into an energy capital, and made petroleum the region's defining industry.
